CONGRANT.TITLE: Future Manufacturing (FM) Seed Grant- Cyber Title “Expanding Manufacturing Capacity in the Rio Grande Valley"
CONTENT_GOAL: GOAL 17: Partnerships to achieve the Goal
GOAL 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Research Description: UTRGVs’ FMSG- CYBER is driven by the concepts developed in our NSF- I-Corps program. The PI’ s experience in this area has shown the institution the value of customer discovery to create viable and applicable research. In this instance the customer discovery that will be pursued with this grant is to explore the available linkages of faculty research capability within the university ecosystem and match that with the capabilities of the local manufacturing industry to capitalize on those skills. By coordinating the functions of each group we will create multiple research streams that will coalesce into real world applications for participating manufacturers. This will be an iterative model. The goal of these iterations will be to have viable research transferred to local manufacturing infrastructure in place to fully utilize the follow on FMRG (Future Manufacturing Research Grants) corollary benefit of this approach will be to explore relationships with technical schools to begin refocusing their training and certifications to meet the needs of the nascent local cyber manufacturing industry.The Chair of Manufacturing and Industrial Engineering will coordinate the research elements between the various research departments. The initially targeted department to conduct the research will be: 1) Department of Manufacturing and Industrial Engineering and the Department of Computer Science at the UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Sciences; and 2) The Department of Information Systems as well as the Department of Entrepreneurship at the College of Business. At least one faculty from each department named will have a related research project which develops targeted technologies that engage small and medium size manufacturers into the ecosystem. These technology concepts (convergent manufacturing and micro factories) are AI driven, with minimal investment requirement, but able to fabricate parts from multiple materials across multiple scale (nano, micro, meso) at the point of need.The Robert Vackar College of Business will be responsible for overseeing the customer discovery, coordination and recruitment of manufacturers and producing research regarding the implementation of cyber manufacturing in a commercialize fashion.

CUE Ethics: Collaborative Research: An Adaptable Discipline-Relevant Introductory Sequence to Build Computational Skills
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Computational knowledge and skills have become essential to all disciplines and economic sectors.  The ubiquity of computing impacts how we educate and prepare the future workforce regardless of one’s chosen career pathway. Thus, it is imperative to develop non-CS undergraduate students’ essential skills in solving problems computationally in their discipline and in possessing knowledge of ethical concerns related to growing cyber threats and vulnerabilities. To address this need, three institutions of higher education are collaborating as a Networked Improvement Community [NIC]: The University of Texas at El Paso [UTEP], Texas A&M University Corpus Christi, and the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.  The aim of improvement at each institution is to raise non-CS students’ motivation to pursue knowledge of computational skills and become aware of ethical and security issues. The proposed project has three objectives to meet its goal of developing non-CS students’ skills for solving problems using computation:  (1) develop and refine outcome-focused, problem-based, discipline-relevant course modules for creating course sequences that are adaptable to varying institutional context and disciplinary degree programs; and (2) incorporate inclusive practices into delivery of the modules to retain and advance students in the computational sequence.

Intellectual Merit. UTEP is the lead institution and Alliance Backbone of the NSF-funded National CAHSI (Computing Alliance for Hispanic-Serving Institutions) INCLUDES Alliance. The Alliance aims to broaden participation of Hispanics in computing using the conditions of collective impact, an improvement science framework closely aligned with NICs. With its 12-year history of building and supporting academic partnerships, CAHSI and its Backbone team are well positioned to support the IHE partnership in the proposed work, which aligns with CAHSI’s mission of growing and sustaining a networked community focused on advancement of Hispanics in computing. The proposed project has defined a collection of modules focused on problem-solving, computational thinking, cybersecurity, and ethics that can be used to create a sequence for STEM, non-CS majors that is adaptable to local context. In addition, the Alliance Backbone will support the professional development of instructors involved in the project with evidence- and research-based inclusive practices, which are especially important for success of Hispanics and other individuals from underrepresented groups. Using the improvement science framework with feedback from the external evaluator, the investigators and STEM subject matter experts from the partner institutions will critically review and iteratively improve organizational structures, course modules, and sequences. The investigators have expertise in working with interdisciplinary projects and are committed to collaborate in refinement of a reconfigurable, introductory course sequence designed to prepare the future STEM workforce with computational knowledge and skills. 

Broader Impacts. The partner institutions are Hispanic-Serving Institutions [HSIs] with majority Hispanic populations. Working with non-CS departments, the project will serve a significant number of women who are over-represented in the partnerships’ STEM fields (other than Physics) involved in the project. This has potential to broaden participation of students from underrepresented groups in computing, a priority of the NSF. The proposed modules are adaptable across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. Because the Alliance operates as a network of networks, it has numerous outlets for disseminating modules to both Alliance institutions and other HSIs. One such outlet is the Alliance’s non-profit-organization partners, Excelencia in Education and Great Minds in STEM, that are national Hispanic organizations sharing a core purpose of increasing the number of Hispanics who are competitive in higher education generally and in computing specifically.

CONGRANT.TITLE: TRUSTVILLE: Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Getting students’ interest piqued in a college degree in a STEM field is challenging. However, due to ever increasing pace of technology transformation, the area of computer science is frequently afforded an opportunity to attract students to relatively new areas with visible impact on everyday life and business. Cyber security, a field pervasively touching almost every aspect of modern life, boasts a promise of job growth of 28% from 2016 through 2026 according to BLS. On the other hand, according to ISACA, 84% of organizations believe that only half or fewer of the applicants for security jobs are qualified. This proposal is for enhancing Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on a Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment (TRUSTVILLE). The proposed integrated security lab, which includes Internet of Things (IOT) equipment as well, will be familiarizing students with the state of the art cyber security appliances and software in a realistic environment to give them a competitive edge in the job market for serving to fill the existing gap in cyber security in public and private sectors.

The Computer Science Department at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley has been offering courses in cyber security area, however, a formal cyber security track with the required training has not been offered due to lack of hardware and software. The institution has Data, Intelligence and Security (DIS) group, with its own lab space, and prides itself for hosting the first International Conference on Data, Intelligence and Security (ICDIS) in April 2018. Given the current faculty expertise in cyber security, experience in teaching related courses, having a DIS group with its own lab space and the market potential for cyber security jobs, the university is strategically poised for offering a specialized track in cyber security to enhance teaching and research.

Due to the market demand, the hardware and software related with cyber security are expensive, and this proposal is for securing funds to assist the institution’s ongoing efforts to establish a market driven cyber security track supported by a modern cyber security integrated laboratory. Since low traffic volume is encountered in a lab environment, expensive high-performance ASIC based hardware is not needed. However, the updates to the firmware and software of security hardware, and to the software itself could be as frequent as daily, for example, to block vulnerabilities including zero-day worms. Therefore, most of the expense of cyber security integrated lab is not in the hardware, but rather in the annual subscription of the software to keep the lab current.

The cyber security track in computer science will consist of seven computer science courses geared towards cyber security, three criminal justice courses, and a senior cornerstone project in the area of cyber security. All of these courses will incorporate Project Based Learning (PBL) methodology to familiarize the students with industry grade cyber security tools and appliances. The required integrated laboratory will consist of a gamut of cyber security related hardware and software to understand and analyze the weaknesses of systems and procedures and learn how to strengthen security at different levels. The integrated security laboratory will consist of software and hardware such as IoT devices, IPS, IDS, threat hunting, vulnerability management, traffic monitoring, penetration testing, forensics, encryption, network security and endpoint security for both on premise and cloud assets.

CONGRANT.TITLE: CUE Ethics: Collaborative Research: An Adaptable Discipline-Relevant
"An Expert Systems Approach to Feature Recognition for Marine ROV Operation with Virtual Reality"
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
During the Summer of 2017, the MSI (Minority Serving Institution) team collaborated with a Maritime Security Center (MSC) Summer Research Institute (SRI) team at Stevens Institute of Technology to develop a low-cost Virtual Reality interface to assist with the operation of an ROV (Remote Operated Vehicle) for maritime homeland security applications.  The proposed research extends this work by adding an expert system for feature recognition to assist with the operation of marine ROVs.  Expertise is provided by Dr. Englot from the MSC at Stevens Institute to the U. of Texas-Rio Grande Valley team, and this expertise is used to develop an expert system that can recognize features such as contraband (drugs, etc.) and IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) that may attached to the hull of ships or placed underwater on pier pilings or other harbor structures.  The methods include classic expert system techniques including: the development of software to manipulate the expertise and interface with the user, elicitation of expertise from a human expert (Dr. Englot), testing of the expert system performance, and documentation of results with the intention to transition this work to an operational application of interest to relevant DHS components.
Through the development and demonstration of this VR (Virtual Reality) system with expert feature recognition, new capabilities are developed that directly support US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) efforts to keep our ports and harbors safe, and eliminate the smuggling of contraband (drugs, etc.).  Currently, ROVs have a significantly poor man-machine interface, and this research offers an opportunity to begin to correct this deficiency, providing better security for our homeland.

CONGRANT.TITLE: UTPA/UTRGV HHMI Leaders in Research Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas Pan American (UTPA) is a Hispanic-serving; Masters I University (Carnegie classification) located in Edinburg, Texas, 10 miles from the U.S.-Mexico border. The 10th largest of 38 public Texas universities, UTPA is growing at a rapid rate with a current enrollment of 19,120 students (16,206 undergraduates) with an 87.7% undergraduate and 79.3% graduate Hispanic population. Student enrolment has increased 9.7% in the last four years and 46.8% in the last 10 years. It is projected that there may be 22,000 students by the end of 2015 and 30,000 by 2020. It is rated among the top 100 as the Best U.S. Colleges for Hispanics including: 3rd in the nation in the number of bachelor’s degrees awarded to Hispanics; 3rd in the number of master’s degrees awarded to Hispanics; 1st in undergraduate degrees awarded to Hispanics in mathematics, and the biological and biomedical sciences [1]. 
Financial support is the largest contributing factor to a UTPA Hispanic student’s success at staying in school and pursuing a science graduate degree. Entering freshman stated that “Financial Aid Availability” and “location” were the top two reasons for attending UTPA [2]. The average poverty rate for the Rio Grande Valley (UTPA location) is 32.2 %, which is significantly higher than the state of Texas poverty rate of 15.4% and the national poverty rate of 12.4% (US Census Bureau, 2000). Currently 58% of UTPA undergraduates have some form of financial aid assistance while 53% of the UTPA student population works part-time [3]. The financial strain that UTPA students are under is reflected in the retention and graduation rates of these students; which in turn leads to a low number of these students pursuing graduate degrees. Nationally, 9.6% of Hispanics complete a bachelor degree compared to 19.3% of white students (US Census Bureau, 2009). This educational rift is even more pronounced at the post baccalaureate level as the percentages of Hispanics earning advanced degrees is 3.6% compared to 10.7% for the white population (US Census Bureau, 2009). Currently, 74.6% of the UTPA student population is first generation college students [4].

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Journal of Computers and Information Science in Engineering
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: This paper investigates the hypothesis that men and women perform differently in virtual environments in terms of balance and coordination during surprise events. It reports on an experiment in human subject balance and coordination using an HTC Vive head-mounted display (HMD) to create a virtual environment. For the experiment, 30 male and 30 female subjects of college age were asked to navigate along a clear path in a virtual world using a controller with their dominant hand and asked to balance a virtual ball on a virtual plate using the other controller in the nondominant hand. The test subjects moved along a clearly marked path, with three surprise obstacles occurring: a large rock landing near the path, an explosion near the path, and a flock of birds coming across the path. Data included six degrees-of-freedom (DOF) trajectories for the head and both hands, as well as data gathered by the computer system on ball location and velocity, plate location and velocity, and ball status. Likert scale questionnaires were answered by the test subjects relative to video game experience, sense of presence, and ease of managing the ball movement. Statistics showed that the male students dropped the ball less frequently at p = 0.0254 and p = 0.0036. In contrast, female students were aware of their performance with correlation levels of 0.632 and 0.588.

INTELLCONT.PUBCTYST: Montreal, Quebec (Virtual Conference due to COVID-19)
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Abstract— With the advent of cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and mobile computing, CS faculty are continuously revamping the curriculum material to address such burgeoning set of technologies in practical and relatable ways. Raspberry Pi (RPi) devices represent an ideal hardware/software framework that embodies all these technologies through its simple architecture, small form factor (that minimizes the volume and footprint of a desktop computer), and ability to integrate various sensors and actuators that network together and connect to the Cloud. Therefore, one of the strategies of Computer Science Department, to enhance depth of learning concepts, has been to infuse Raspberry Pi (RPi) in computer science courses. RPi has been incorporated since 2017 in targeted courses, notably, Computer Organization & Assembly Language, Computer Architecture, Database Management Design & Implementation, Unix/Linux Programming, Internet Programming, and Senior Project. An inexpensive credit card sized computer, an RPi lends itself to allow depth of learning of concepts. From implementing firewalls,intrusion detection systems, scripting, client-server based computing, distributed computing, to interfacing with sensors and actuators, a student is guided to polish concepts taught in a class through RPi Project Based Learning (RPBL). Computer science curriculum already provides breadth of learning. The infusion of RPi in key courses provides depth in targeted concepts. There are peripheral desirable consequences as well, including a student learning prevalently used Linux environment even though a targeted course may have nothing directly to do with Linux.Furthermore, RPi provides an opportunity for students to realize that software programs can be interfaced with sensors and actuators to provide immersed experience in programming. From simply interfacing a switch and a Light Emitting Diode (LED) to getting data from sensors,buffering, and uploading to the cloud, a student already would have touched upon multiple disciplines in computer science. This paper provides a blueprint to infusing RPi in the targeted courses, and how each RPi based project provides depth to a targeted concept.

Index Terms—Raspberry Pi, Cloud Computing, Internet of Things (IoT), Mobile Computing, Linux.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Applying Deep Q-Learning and Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Options to Agents in Exploratory Games
INTELLCONT.TITLE_SECONDARY: Proceedings of the 2018 AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: UTRGV
UTRGV
University of Connecticut

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: AAAI
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Following the high-profile applications of Deep Learning to Atari video games (Mnih et al., 2015) and the classic game Go (Silver et al., 2016), there has been considerable momentum and interest in Deep Q-Learning (DQN), leading to a steady stream of advances and new application. However, in the area of video game agents, the default application continues to be strategy and reactive skill optimization, leaving opportunity to explore how these advancing techniques can be applied to other agent goals. In this work, we look at the gather-craft cycle as a starting point for exploratory games in general, to see how DQN and related Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) can advance learning flexible and reusable behaviors for agents that don’t target globally optimal policies.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Extraction of Interaction Events for Learning Reasonable Behavior in an Open-World Survival Game
INTELLCONT.TITLE_SECONDARY: The Workshops of the The Thirty-Second AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: AAAI
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Extracting event knowledge from open-world survival video games is a promising domain to investigate the application of Machine Learning techniques to routine human decision making. This contrasts with and builds upon typical game-based decision making work that focuses on optimal behavior. We propose an Interaction Graph data structure that can be trained from game play to enable hybrid reasoning and statistical estimation about what events can happen in the world. This enables an agent to exhibit increasingly more reasonable behavior after low numbers of training runs. An implementation and initial experimental validation are presented.

SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.DESC: Asked to continue as Interim Chair by the Dean.
SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.ACCOMPLISH:
One critical Tenure Track faculty hire and two 3-yr Lecturer hires in Spring 2019, successful late-summer hires to cover all classes on both campuses. All classes on both campuses made enrollment, nearly all undergraduate classes in Edinburg were full, and most waitlist demand was satisfied. Strong, consistent growth at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, including over 20k funded WSCH for the first time (including our 50% of the CMPE program).
 
We increased research time for our first-year faculty, and saw another successful large grant (Dr. Kim, USDA, $350,000).

SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.DESC: Asked to serve as Interim Chair by the Dean in May 2017 (confirmed by faculty vote) and to continue by the new Dean in March 2018.
SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.ACCOMPLISH:
Three critical Tenure Track faculty hires in Spring 2018, successful late-summer hires to cover all classes on both campuses, all classes on both campuses are now making enrollment, and after two years of not being able to meet all student demand in Edinburg, we cleared all waitlists for Fall 2018, in spite of a reduction in teaching capacity. We have strong, consistent undergraduate (9% overall, 5% on the Brownsville campus) and graduate (6%) program growth (based on Fall SCHs). 

We also increased research time and resources for Tenure Track and highly research productive faculty, and increased external funding ($50k/1yr Dr. Tomai (with Dr. Alley Butler, MANE), $500k/3yr Dr. Schweller and Dr. Wylie).

SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.DESC: Coordinate design, collection and evaluation of assessment data for CSCI 1380 core course.

Responsible to evaluate and approve student external internships for course credit (CSCI/CMPE 3300), disseminate information about the internship course, coordinate with internship supervisors to collect responsibilities and evaluation letters, coordinate with students to accept, evaluate and approve or reject mid-term and final reports.

SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.ACCOMPLISH: Significant reworking of BSCS degree pre-requisites, clean up of degree errors from UTRGV transition, discussion of future degree simplification.

SERVICE_DEPARTMENT.DESC: At the direction of the chair, I handled hiring and assignments for our undergraduate instructional support students, who assist with our introductory lab courses.

- Organize processes and create documents for advising.
- Coordinate scheduling between the CSCI and CMPE.
- Liason for cross-department course offering and scheduling.
- Resolve all unusual advising and registration issues.
- Handle all course substitution requests.
- Transfer advisement and resolution of transfer issues.
- Administer CSCI and CMPE internship courses.
- Administer senior exit surveys/exams for CSCI and CMPE.
- Assist in leading general accreditation activities.
Got access to the CSCI website, learned the CMS and performed content updates.

SERVICE_COLLEGE.DESC: Participated in collaborative College planning and operation as an Interim Chair.
Bi-weekly meetings all year to review UTPA, UTRGV and external HOP, policies, and bylaws, and to draft, discuss and edit COEC bylaws.
SERVICE_COLLEGE.ACCOMPLISH: Drafted first UTRGV COEC college bylaws.

SERVICE_UNIVERSITY.DESC: Organized two targeted campus recruiting visits and a webinar series from Google, Inc including mock interviews, a resume workshop, a technical presentation and a career presentation.
SERVICE_UNIVERSITY.ACCOMPLISH: After being contacted by them, I worked with Google representatives, with the help and support of Career Services and the UTRGV ACM student organization to arrange two visits last year. Roughly 80-100 students attended the activities each time.

SERVICE_PUBLIC.DESC: Co-organized outreach to elementary/middle school teachers with Continuing Ed to provide training and support for after-school coding clubs.
SERVICE_PUBLIC.ACCOMPLISH:
Trained and supported 30 elementary and middle school teachers in the Harlingen and PSJA districts, impacting over 180 students with weekly club meetings from Oct to Apr.

Students learned Scratch programming and competed in two challenge competitions across the districts.

Secured Google, Inc, as a sponsor who provided challenge prizes and Q&A videos answering student questions.

Organized an end-of-year summit with ~200 students, teachers and family members in attendance for the final challenge judging and hands-on activities.

Funded two UTRGV undergrads to provide teacher support.

SERVICE_PUBLIC.DESC: Participated in Treasure Hills Elementary coding night outreach to students and parents. Presented principles of computer science and ran unplugged activities. Roughly 40 families in attendance.
I recruited and coordinated with three local troops of Girl Scouts to come to a one-day workshop at the new UTRGV FabLab where we introduced them to digital fabrication technology and coding.

SERVICE_PUBLIC.ORG: Brownsville ISD "Girls Can Code" Camp Collaboration
SERVICE_PUBLIC.DESC: I worked with the Office of Continuing Education to support a Brownsville ISD summer coding camp for middle school girls. I put together a team of UTRGV CSCI and CMPE students and guided them in developing a four-week curriculum for the camp, which they then trained and supported BISD teachers on delivering.
